Visuals.all: Coherent, recognisable city with consistent art direction: textured brick and stone facades, Gothic church detail, market stalls, bikes and railings, real-time shadows and warm low-sun lighting with some atmospheric haze. But geometry is mostly boxy and low-detail, the shop interiors use primitive shapes, materials are flat and repetitive, and there is little clutter or vegetation. Characters are simple, chunky low-poly figures, and the bell boss and enemies look toy-like. It sits clearly below the 60 anchor for character detail and lighting richness.

Animation.all: In the walking shots the player is seen from behind in nearly the same stride each time, with the staff held at slightly different angles. That points to a basic walk cycle at most, with no visible secondary motion on the robe or hat. In combat the attacks show up almost entirely as projectiles, rings, spikes and damage numbers. The player's body barely changes pose, and 'STAGGERED' and 'INTERRUPTED' appear only as text, not as visible hit reactions. The bell boss shifts its arms between a few poses, but there are no clear wind-ups, death animations or follow-through. Pedestrians stand in place and nothing in the environment moves.

Combat feel.hexweaver: There is clear evidence of real combat. The boss has three phases and named, telegraphed attacks (Great Toll, Clapper Sweep, Change-Ringing Cascade, an enrage state and ground circles). Floating damage and crit numbers, STAGGERED and chain-combo indicators, 6 distinct spells with cooldowns, loot with rarity tiers and 6883 sound voices all point to working hit feedback. The biggest gaps: the boss fight is a cluttered blob of overlapping VFX right next to the player, with no visible hit-stop, knockback or screen feedback. The spell shapes don't read as distinct, crowd control isn't seen changing the fight, and only one class is shown, so differences between classes can't be judged.
Combat feel.pyromancer: The pyromancer uses six distinct spells, and the frames show the supporting systems: damage numbers including crits, STAGGERED states, chain counters and a named boss with three phases. The boss also shows ground telegraphs and named attacks (Clapper Sweep, Peal of Shards, Great Toll), and loot drops come in common, uncommon and rare tiers. The VFX are mostly flat white or orange blobs and bloom washes that hide the action (frames 5 and 10), and there's no visible hit-stop, knockback or exciting loot moments. Only one class appears on this sheet, so differences between classes can't be judged.
Combat feel.stormcaller: The fight shows real combat feedback: a bellwarden boss with three named phases, an enrage state, named and telegraphed attacks (Great Toll, Clapper Sweep, Peal of Shards) with red ground markers, STAGGERED/INTERRUPTED states, crit numbers, a chain counter, rarity-coloured loot beams and low-health/death screens. The biggest gaps are readability and impact. The boss and the large target reticle often cover the player, the spell effects look washed out and hard to tell apart, and there is no visible hit-stop or strong impact. The player died twice to a boss doing only a modest 16 hits, which suggests weak counterplay, and the enemies show no clear formations.
Combat feel.warden: The warden uses six distinct spells, including crowd control and a leap. Hits show damage numbers and status labels such as STAGGERED and INTERRUPTED, and a named boss telegraphs attacks with ground markers (Belfry Drop, Peal of Shards) and moves into phase II. Loot appears as beams with rarity colours, and the low-health screen tint and combo chain counter add feedback. Clutter is the main weakness: rocks and geometry block the camera in frames 1 and 9, VFX shapes are often muddy, and only 1 crit landed. No hit-stop is visible, pebble_shot makes up most casts, none of the 14 drops was picked up, and only one class can be judged from this clip.

Story presentation.all: The story presentation is strong for its scope. Dialogue uses letterboxed over-the-shoulder shots with portraits, speaker names and roles, and there are branching reply choices, title cards, a boss reveal shot and a quest-complete reward screen. The writing is flavourful and ties the quest to real Cambridge locations (Market Hill, Great St Mary's). The biggest gaps: the characters are simple chibi models with no visible expressive animation or lip-sync, there is no evidence of voice acting, the portraits are generic icons, and no quest marker or waypoint appears in the world, so it falls short of fully staged cinematic performances.

UI polish.all: The UI has one consistent dark-and-gold serif theme across the class selection, inventory, talents and HUD. The HUD reads clearly, with numeric cooldowns on icon spell slots, a styled boss bar with phase labels, rarity-coloured gear slots and a collection tracker, and clearly organised talent tiers. It loses points because the HUD is small and fairly generic. The talent and inventory screens are dense, text-heavy panels with small type. During fights, damage numbers, the targeting reticle and effects pile up in the centre of the screen. These are still frames, so there is no evidence of animation or transitions.
